rules.title: Writable folder in root's PATH
rules.subject: {scope}: {dir}
rules.why: Root looks up commands in these folders. A program planted in a writable one under the name of a command root runs, ahead of the real one or in place of a missing one, runs as root.
rules.fix: Remove the folder from root's PATH (sudo secure_path, /etc/environment, /etc/login.defs, the PATH line in /etc/crontab) or make it owned by root and writable only by root.

rules.title: Missing folder in root's PATH can be created by non-root users
rules.subject: {scope}: {dir}
rules.why: The folder doesn't exist, but non-root users can create it, and then plant commands that root will find through its PATH.
rules.fix: Remove the stale entry from root's PATH, or create the folder owned by root and writable only by root.

rules.title: Relative or empty entry in root's PATH
rules.subject: {scope}: {dir}
rules.why: An empty or relative PATH entry means 'the current folder', so root runs whatever program of the right name sits in whichever folder it happens to be working in.
rules.fix: Remove the entry (look for '.', a leading or trailing ':', or '::').

rules.title: Windows folders are in root's PATH (WSL)
rules.subject: appendWindowsPath
rules.why: WSL appends the Windows PATH to every Linux account's PATH, root's included. Every account in the distro, and anything running as your Windows user, can write to those folders, so a command root can't find in the Linux folders may run from there instead.
rules.fix: Set appendWindowsPath = false under [interop] in /etc/wsl.conf, then run wsl --shutdown. Add the few Windows tools you need to PATH by hand.

rules.title: Account or authentication file can be modified
rules.subject: {path}
rules.why: These files decide who the accounts are, what their passwords are and who may use sudo. Whoever can change one can give themselves root.
rules.fix: Restore the standard ownership and modes: root:root 644 for passwd and group, root:shadow 640 (or 600) for shadow and gshadow, root:root 440 for sudoers, root:root 755 for /etc/sudoers.d and /etc/pam.d.

rules.title: Password hashes are readable
rules.subject: {path}
rules.why: Anyone who can read the password hashes can try to crack them offline, including root's.
rules.fix: Make the file owned by root (group shadow on Debian-family systems) and not readable by others: chmod 640 or 600. Delete stale backup copies.

rules.title: Configuration that root runs automatically can be modified
rules.subject: {path}
rules.why: Root reads this to decide what to run on a schedule, at boot, or inside every program it starts (the dynamic loader settings). Whoever can change it runs code as root.
rules.fix: Make it owned by root and writable only by root (chown root:root, chmod 644 for files, 755 for folders).

rules.title: Shell startup file used by root can be modified
rules.subject: {path}
rules.why: Login shells, including root's, run these files at startup. Whoever can change one runs code as root the next time an administrator logs in or opens a root shell.
rules.fix: Make it owned by root and writable only by root (chown root:root, chmod 644 for files, 755 for /etc/profile.d).

rules.title: root's home folder is readable by other users
rules.subject: {path}
rules.why: root's home holds its shell history, SSH keys and other credentials. Other users shouldn't be able to list it.

rules.title: NFS export disables root squashing
rules.subject: {line}
rules.why: With no_root_squash, root on any client that mounts this export is also root on its files, so a compromised or untrusted client can plant setuid programs that run as root here.
rules.fix: Remove no_root_squash (root_squash is the default) and re-export with exportfs -ra.

rules.title: Library preloaded into every program can be overwritten
rules.subject: {path}
rules.why: Libraries listed in /etc/ld.so.preload are loaded into every program, setuid-root programs included. Whoever can overwrite one runs code as root.
rules.fix: Make the library owned by root and writable only by root, and check that it belongs there: a preload entry is unusual on most systems.

rules.title: Library folder in the loader configuration lets non-root users add files
rules.subject: {dir}
rules.why: Programs, including ones that run as root, load shared libraries from the folders in the loader configuration. A library planted under the right name runs inside them.
rules.fix: Make the folder owned by root and writable only by root, or remove it from the loader configuration and run ldconfig.

rules.title: Container engine socket is writable
rules.subject: {path}
rules.why: Whoever can talk to this socket controls a container engine running as root, and can start a container with the host's filesystem mounted. That is root on the host.
rules.fix: Keep the socket root:root (or root:docker with only administrators in the docker group), mode 660. Consider rootless Docker or Podman.
